context_chunks.text: Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. Rollout plan: feature-flagged behind feature.enable_multipart_input (off by default); staged rollout to internal dogfood tenants, then gradual roll to 10%, 50%, 100% via config rollout.

Checklist: - [x] Streaming-safe multipart parser implemented - [x] Content-Type whitelist + validation errors - [x] Per-file and per-request size enforcement + configurable defaults - [x] OpenAI-compat error mapping and structured error shapes - [x] Tests: unit, integration, e2e - [x] Docs: compatibility notes and config guide - [x] Telemetry: counters for rejected parts and throttled requests - [x] Migration & rollout plan included Testing notes: the multipart parser uses a small constant memory footprint for each active part and yields part metadata to the handler; large parts trigger a streaming drain with early termination (413 response) to avoid OOM. Integration tests exercise combination of binary and text parts, wrong content-types, and boundary cases around the configured limits. Telemetry: added metrics api.multipart.rejected_content_type, api.multipart.rejected_size, api.multipart.accepted_parts and a hist for part sizes. Implementation details: - parser: runtime/multipart/stream_parser.py - validator: api/validation/multipart_validator.py - compat layer: api/openai_compat/input_adapter.py - config: config/defaults/multipart.yaml - docs: docs/openai-compat/multipart.md - tests: tests/unit/test_multipart_parser.py, tests/integration/test_openai_compat_multipart.py Error shape examples (structured output): when a part is rejected we return 413 with a JSON body {"error":{"type":"request_too_large","message":"part exceeds max_file_size","meta":{"part_name":"file","limit_bytes":10485760}}} and 400 for unsupported content-types with type unsupported_media_type. Observability: trace spans added around parse->validate->route dispatch to help pinpoint latency regressions.

Motivation: Close a set of subtle incompatibilities between our /v1/chat.completions adapter and OpenAI's behavior that have been causing developer friction in streaming function-call flows and stop/logprobs handling. This PR implements a compact 'parameter normalizer' layer and a streaming framing/backpressure handshake to make the adapter tolerant of real-world clients and OpenAI-style payloads. Summary of changes: - Parameter normalizer: unify and sanitize incoming params (max_tokens, temperature, top_p, n, presence_penalty) and map them to our internal API consistently; accept both string and numeric encodings, preserve explicit nulls, and prefer client-provided values for edge cases. - Role aliasing: accept and normalize role names coming from clients ("assistant", "system", "user", "tool", and legacy aliases like "ai" or "bot"); ensure role is preserved in both final and streaming envelopes. - Stop sequence deduplication: support stop as string or array; expand single-string stops into an array; dedupe overlapping sequences (e.g. ["

", "


"]) and maintain order stability to match OpenAI semantics. - Sparse logprobs: add an opt-in sparse_logprobs mode that mirrors OpenAI's sparse token-level logprob structure when requested; keep heavy-weight computation behind an explicit flag to avoid perf regressions. - Streaming framing & backpressure: introduce a light handshake in the stream start (sent as first SSE/delta) that communicates our token framing and heartbeat expectations; implement backpressure signaling for HTTP/2 clients to avoid partial JSON objects when a client pauses mid-stream. - Function-call streaming support: improve chunking for function_call.name/arguments so that streaming deltas assemble deterministically into valid JSON payloads even across reconnects; final chunk action inserts a stable end-of-function marker to make reconstruction robust.

- Deterministic intent: include all inputs that can affect output (tokenizer, seed, model artifact id, runtime config, injected policies). - Portable: JSON-compatible, human-readable, and easy to attach to support tickets or GitHub issues. - Privacy-aware: fields that may contain PII must be flagged and optionally replaced with redaction pointers. **Customer content (MUST remain within pinned region(s))**
- Prompt / messages / input text (including system prompts provided by customer)
- Tool/function call arguments provided by customer
- Uploaded documents or retrieved passages (RAG payloads) provided by customer
- Model outputs (including partial streaming tokens)
- Embeddings input text and embeddings vectors derived from customer text
- Rerank inputs (candidate passages) and rerank outputs derived from those passages
- Fine-tuning / adapter payloads if routed through Hosted API pathways (not in scope for v1 feature, but classification applies)
- Any debug payloads that include raw request/response bodies
- Any derived artifacts that can reconstruct content (e.g., token logs, decoded segments, sampled prompt fragments)

**Not customer content (may be processed outside pinned region(s) under constraints below)**
- Non-content operational metadata that does not include request/response bodies and cannot reasonably be used to reconstruct them (see “Allowed cross-region metadata”). Notes:
- Whether content includes PII is not determinative; **all prompts/outputs are treated as sensitive content**. - “Derived” includes transformations (tokenization, embedding vectors, compression) if they are computed from customer text/output. ### 2) Enforcement boundary: “Where residency applies”
For pinned orgs/projects/API keys, **all handling of customer content** must remain in allowed region(s) for:
- **Request routing** and execution (including retries and fallbacks)
- **Background work** that uses the request payload or output (e.g., async logging of bodies, eval capture, replay queues)
- **Persistence and caching** of any form of request/response content
- **Observability signals** that contain content (logs/traces/debug captures)

Residency enforcement is evaluated at request time by the gateway/routing policy engine and must be **deterministic** (same policy + same request context → same allow/block outcome).

Motivation: Customers using the OpenAI Responses family expect stable streaming semantics, reliable tool/function call signal delivery, and preservation of determinism hints (seed/RNG) and user metadata when we bridge from our internal Responses v9-compatible runtime to the OpenAI API shape. This PR adds a resilience layer that: 1) performs backpressure-aware chunking and reassembly for streaming frames to avoid partial json/toolcall corruption on slow clients, 2) proxies a lightweight 'tool-signal' envelope so function/tool-calling boundaries are deterministic across retries and reconnections, and 3) forwards seed/determinism flags and a subset of user metadata transparently through the compatibility layer. What this changes (summary): consistent chunk framing and reassembly on the server and client-facing bridge; explicit tool-signal envelope that annotates tool-call start/end + unique tool invocation id; passthrough of 'rng_seed' and 'deterministic' attributes from our Responses request model into the OpenAI-compatible response attributes; metadata routing (user-provided tags/trace id) added to response attributes and to audit logs so downstream services (console, evals) see the same identifiers. Compatibility notes: We keep the OpenAI-compatible surface stable for existing callers. Default behavior is identical unless callers set determinism/seed or rely on streaming reconnects; in those cases the bridge guarantees idempotent framing (replay-safe chunk markers) and consistent toolcall reassembly. There are small opt-ins: the 'tool-signal' envelope is only applied when callers include a 'enable_tool_signal' flag (default true for our hosted API). For private deployments customers can opt-out via config.

The new metric added to allow SRE to track when server-side streaming sessions are finalized due to hitting a time limit is the **`__redwood_timeboxed__`** structured terminal event [1].

This was implemented as part of a server-side streaming timebox (which is configurable per-route) to provide a "predictable server-side safety net" that converts oversized or in-flight streams into a final event when they exceed a configured residency time [1, 2].

context_chunks.text: Context: production customers observed cases where long lived streaming sessions (tool calls + structured output) were left in indeterminate states after a client network disconnect or a client-initiated Cancel. Motivation: we need a predictable server-side safety net that bounds resource residency time, ensures tool-call idempotency when retries/resume occur, and provides a clear fallback path (trimmed response + final event) that OpenAI-compatible clients can rely on. This PR implements a server-side streaming timebox (configurable per-route) that gracefully converts oversized/inflight streams into a final 'timeboxed' terminal event, augments client-cancel handling to be idempotent across reconnect/resume windows, and plumbs a compact resume token that includes tool-call idempotency metadata. Summary of changes: 1) stream manager: add configurable timebox_ms and a deterministic finalization path that emits a structured terminal event ("__redwood_timeboxed__") with a compact summary; 2) openai adapter: interpret Cancel events as idempotent markers tied to resume tokens; retries within the resume window will deduplicate tool calls using a request-level id; 3) tooling: map function-call invocations to idempotency keys and persist minimal call metadata to the stream checkpoint to support safe resume; 4) API: extend the OpenAI-compat streaming spec with two optional fields in the final event (timeboxed=true, resume_hint) without breaking existing clients; 5) tests & docs: integration tests for flaky network simulated disconnects and release notes for the behavior and recommended operational knobs. Rollout plan: feature guarded behind a runtime flag and route-level config. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is unchanged unless a route opts-in. Checklist: [x] unit tests for stream finalizer [x] integration test that simulates disconnect + resume [x] docs page and compatibility notes [x] change log entry. Related: ENG-1023 (stream lifecycle SLO), SUP-4572 (customer incident replicant).

Marcus Li (2026-02-21): Fixed by injecting a deterministic clock to the stream finalizer and making the resume window configurable for tests. Reran CI locally. SRE Team (CI bot) (2026-02-24): One lint failure in openai_compat_stream.go for an unused variable — fixed in follow-up commit. Ava Chen (2026-02-24): Approved after last fixes. Marking as ready to merge. Server-side streaming timebox (route-configurable) that guarantees a graceful terminal event when streams exceed a configured residency time. Client Cancel events are now idempotent within a short resume window; resume tokens include minimal idempotency hints to avoid duplicated tool/function executions on reconnect. Default behavior unchanged unless enabled per-route.

Summary:

On 2026-04-25 at ~02:12 UTC the hosted streaming API experienced a high-severity outage that manifested as 5xx errors for streaming sessions and extreme tail latency for non-streaming requests. Impact lasted ~43 minutes for customers on affected regions and degraded for another 90 minutes during mitigation rollouts. Root cause: an unintended change to a per-connection TTL/keepalive config combined with an edge buffer write-stall bug in the streaming proxy, which caused head-of-line stalls and backlog amplification under normal traffic spikes.

Impact:
- Scope: ~11% of streaming sessions experienced repeated 5xx (502/504) immediately; additional ~7% of non-streaming requests saw 95th+ latency spikes from 600ms -> 3.2s.
- Customers: 23 enterprise tenants saw visible error rates; a handful of PLG customers reported degraded developer experience. No data loss or model correctness issues were observed.
- Business: Incidents triggered PagerDuty P0 and on-call SREs initiated incident response. External status page was updated.

How it was detected:
- First alert: custom anomaly detector on streaming session error-rate crossed threshold at 02:13 UTC (SRE paging).
- Secondary signals: edge response-time dashboards and increased connection resets observed in edge logs.
- Pager: 02:14 UTC, SRE lead ack at 02:15 UTC.

Timeline (UTC):
- 02:12 — initial spike in streaming session errors; error rate rose from baseline 0.3% to 18% in 2 minutes.
- 02:13 — anomaly alert fires; on-call SRE starts investigation.
- 02:14 — correlating logs show write stall metrics on streaming proxy (high write queue depth).
- 02:18 — quick mitigation: rolling restart of streaming-proxy fleet in affected region, partial drop in errors but tail latency persisted.
- 02:25 — rollback of a recent edge-config change that adjusted connection TTL made at 01:55 UTC.

- Customer confirmed jitter reduced the “all-at-once” failure mode. - 2026-03-20 (post 1.14.1-rc2 canary + reserved burst config still in place):
  - No sustained 429s for /v1/chat during the 09:00–10:00 window. - A few 429s remain on background /v1/embed chunk callbacks (expected; acceptable if retried with backoff). Open questions / TODO
- Edge proxy: ensure X-RateLimit headers are emitted even under backpressure for 429s originating from rate-limiter. - Confirm whether signed URL callback endpoints should be assigned their own priority class (e.g., “callback-low”) distinct from generic background. - Add a regression test: attach burst + high fanout + two priority classes should never allow cross-pool borrow that depletes interactive tokens. Recommended next steps (updated plan)
1) Keep the reserved interactive burst split (30%) for dedicated pools with mixed interactive + bulk ingest traffic. 2) Promote rate-limiter 1.14.1 from rc to stable after 48h canary observation (watch: rlim.route.tokens.available deltas, interactive 429 rate, attach timing). 3) Edge proxy change: always populate rate-limit headers (or at least a stable error code) for 429s; avoid “opaque 429”. 4) Update the support playbook page with explicit guidance for signed URL callback fanout (jitter + concurrency caps + route separation). 5) Schedule a controlled load test with Streamly AI for 3 consecutive peak windows and collect traces + request IDs for closure criteria. Notes / timeline crumbs (for internal use)
- 2026-03-10: incident window; strong correlation with cron flush. - 2026-03-11: Eng suspected weight inversion / attach sequence sensitivity. - 2026-03-12: customer call; implemented burst reservation + client-side jitter. - 2026-03-19: 1.14.1-rc2 canary deployed to us-west dedicated. - 2026-03-20: customer reports no sustained interactive 429s during flush. Closure criteria (for SUP-864999)
- Interactive endpoints (/v1/chat) see <0.1% 429 during scheduled flush windows for 3 consecutive days.

Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)

- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots

- Deterministic intent: include all inputs that can affect output (tokenizer, seed, model artifact id, runtime config, injected policies). - Portable: JSON-compatible, human-readable, and easy to attach to support tickets or GitHub issues. - Privacy-aware: fields that may contain PII must be flagged and optionally replaced with redaction pointers. Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

- host_os: ubuntu-22.04
- runtime_image: redwood/runtime-infer:2025-10-21

Inputs / data model assumptions

  - signals (per region, per signal type):

    - errors_5xx_burn: burn_rate + window + confidence
    - tail_latency_burn: burn_rate + p95/p99 deltas + confidence
    - capacity_headroom: percent + “hard gate” boolean
    - control_plane_health (optional): ok|degraded|down
  - evaluation_time (UTC epoch + monotonic sequence)
  - constraints (policy-level + tenant-level): max_flips_per_hour, min_hold_down_seconds, require_approval, blast_radius_limit

Determinism requirements (core)
1) Stable ordering
- Evaluation must not depend on map iteration order. - Rule matching must define explicit ordering: by priority, then by tie-breakers. 2) Stable time semantics
- All windowed signals must be anchored to evaluation_time and include:
  - effective_start, effective_end, and a “freshness” timestamp. - Engine must treat stale signals consistently:
  - If authoritative signals are stale beyond threshold, decision = HOLD (do not fail over) unless reachability is explicitly DOWN with high confidence. 3) Single decision per evaluation
- For a given (route_id, tenant_id, evaluation_time), engine emits exactly one decision object, even if multiple actions are possible. - Multi-step actions (e.g., drain -> shift weights -> finalize) must be represented as a sequence recommendation but still within a single decision record.

The proposed canonical priority order for evaluating different failure signals (Signal hierarchy evaluation, ADR-042) is as follows:

1.  **Reachability DOWN (authoritative):** Results in a **FAILOVER** (unless there is no healthy fallback) [2].
2.  **Errors (5xx) fast burn (high severity):** Results in a **FAILOVER** or **PARTIAL_SHIFT**, depending on capacity and blast radius [2].
3.  **Tail latency burn (p99/p95):** Results in a **PARTIAL_SHIFT** first; it escalates to a **FAILOVER** if the signal is sustained and corroborated [2].
4.  **Capacity exhaustion / hard gate:** Results in a **HOLD** + load shed (controller action) to avoid shifting traffic into a constrained region [2].
5.  **Control plane degradation:** Results in a **HOLD** to prevent rapid flipping and oscillation [2].

Context / what changed since the Confluence version
-----------------------------------------------
This is a working doc intended to supersede the older Confluence page for day-to-day ops. Key updates vs. Confluence (note to reviewers):
- We standardized on p95 + error-rate for decision gates; p99 is still tracked but no longer the primary gate except for cross-region routing tests. - Cross-region routing cost model updated: egress is now tracked per "GiB" from the provider bill and attributed back to request traces by sampled bytes (we can’t reliably infer from tokens alone). - CLI note: "redwoodctl" commands are still mostly correct, but platform tooling is being migrated to "rfctl". Keep both until Q2. - Added explicit "customer harm" metrics: support ticket rate + HTTP 429/5xx annotations for throttling experiments. Overview
========

This document captures a reproducible experiment matrix for operator-driven fallback strategies and an associated cost-penalty catalog used to evaluate trade-offs between SLO preservation and unit economics across regional surges. Intended audience: platform operators, SREs, runtime engineers, and product engineers running controlled degradation experiments or designing automatic fallback policies. Why this exists
---------------
- Fallbacks preserve SLOs during capacity scarcity or model regressions, but they can change cost, quality, and customer experience. - Operators need a concise experiment plan with metrics, dashboard queries, and a cost penalty model to compare candidate strategies. - We want a single template for telemetry, rollout/rollback steps, and decision criteria for productionizing fallbacks. Goals and scope
---------------
- Goal: Repeatable experiment matrix yielding quantitative comparisons of: latency SLO retention, token-cost delta, quality regressions (evals), and operator intervention effort. - Scope: Multiregion inference surface (hosted + dedicated), model variant fallbacks (quantized, smaller model families), routing degradations (regional drain, tenant throttling).

**Detection:**

**Response:**
- Disabled failover automation for the scoped policy (feature flag / controller disable). - Reduced gateway retry pressure using existing runtime/gateway knobs (temporary tuning) while traffic re-stabilized. - Confirmed eu-west capacity headroom and verified no persistent impairment. - Coordinated comms with Support: acknowledged planned test, explained transient errors, offered retry guidance. ## Root cause
The regression was caused by **policy oscillation** (flip/rollback) triggered by **noisy reachability signals**, combined with insufficient guardrails that allowed multiple routing policy changes in a short period. The oscillation produced a traffic pattern that:
1) **increased cross-region redirects**, and
2) **amplified retries** at the gateway/client level,
leading to transient overload and elevated error rates in the target region. Key technical drivers:
- **Reachability probes produced false positives** (brief, correlated failures) that were treated as authoritative without adequate corroboration. - **Hold-down and anti-flap timers were too permissive** for the observed signal volatility. - **Rollback semantics were correct per implementation**, but not aligned with our intended ADR-level behavior (we rolled back too quickly and re-triggered failover immediately).

## Overview
This page is the current internal FAQ for answering enterprise buyer questions about purchasing Redwood Inference through AWS Marketplace (public offer vs private offer), and the most common security/compliance questions (SOC 2, encryption/KMS, retention, audit logs, data residency, incident response, and SSO/RBAC). This content is used by AEs/SEs for deals where the customer prefers AWS Marketplace so spend can count toward AWS commitments (e.g., EDP) and to streamline vendor onboarding. ---

## What customers typically ask for (quick list)
- Why buy via AWS Marketplace (EDP/committed spend, consolidated invoicing) and when to use a private offer. - SKU fit: Hosted API now, Dedicated capacity later, and when Private (VPC) is required. - Metering and billing: dimensions (tokens/requests), reporting cadence, and invoice visibility. - Security questionnaire items: SOC 2 posture, encryption/KMS, retention controls, audit logs, data residency, incident response, and SSO/RBAC. - Shared responsibility boundaries for Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private. - Onboarding flow: subscription → entitlement validation → org provisioning/linking → first API key → first call. - Support and escalation expectations for marketplace customers. ---

## Marketplace procurement FAQ

### Q: Public offer or private offer? **Recommended for enterprise: Private offer.** Private offers allow us to align term length, committed spend constructs, and any deal-specific exhibits (e.g., security addendum, DPA references) while still using Marketplace as the procurement channel. **Public offer** (pay-as-you-go) is typically used for small pilots or when procurement does not require an order-form-like artifact. ### Q: Does Marketplace spend count toward AWS commitments (e.g., EDP)? In most enterprise cases **yes**, but eligibility is determined by the customer’s AWS agreement and how the offer is accepted. When asked, we should state:
- We structure offers using standard AWS Marketplace constructs. - The customer should confirm EDP crediting mechanics with their AWS account team.

Determinism requirements (core)
1) Stable ordering
- Evaluation must not depend on map iteration order. - Rule matching must define explicit ordering: by priority, then by tie-breakers. 2) Stable time semantics
- All windowed signals must be anchored to evaluation_time and include:

- For a given (route_id, tenant_id, evaluation_time), engine emits exactly one decision object, even if multiple actions are possible. - Multi-step actions (e.g., drain -> shift weights -> finalize) must be represented as a sequence recommendation but still within a single decision record.

The new alerting approach groups model-serving requests by creating "stage-aware cohorts" to reduce noise and accelerate root cause analysis (RCA) through the following methods:

*   **Cohort Creation via Stage Footprints:** The approach uses a lightweight `token_stage_cohort` service to compute a deterministic cohort key for every invocation. This key is based on a "stage footprint," which includes stage-level metrics such as token counts per stage, kv-cache hit patterns, and decode-batch size [1].
*   **Reducing Alert Noise:** Instead of traditional per-route and per-quantile alerts, the system uses an alert route-matrix generator. This generator consumes cohort rollups and emits alert bindings that "bias escalation to the top-k stages" for a given route [1]. Additionally, the system includes "automatic quiet-window attenuation" to prevent regressing noise during the rollout [1].
*   **Speeding up RCA:** The approach attributes SLO violations to the most likely pipeline stage by deriving a "route x stage alert matrix" [1]. To assist on-call engineers in validating root cause hypotheses, a new dashboard is provided that focuses on per-cohort cost/latency breakdowns, stage heatmaps, and cohort drift [1].

context_chunks.text: Context: long-tail token cost and multi-stage latency spikes frequently surface only when a request traverses several model-serving stages (tokenization, encoder, decode, fallback). Existing alerts were per-route and per-quantile but lacked a compact way to group requests by 'stage footprint' and automatically route alerting weight to the stage(s) most likely responsible. Motivation: reduce alert noise and accelerate RCA by grouping invocations into stage-aware cohorts and deriving a route x stage alert matrix that attributes SLO violations to the most likely pipeline stage. What this PR does: 1) Adds a lightweight token_stage_cohort service that computes a deterministic cohort key per invocation based on stage-level metrics (token counts per stage, kv-cache hit pattern, decode-batch size) and stores short-lived cohort aggregates. 2) Introduces an alert route-matrix generator that consumes cohort rollups and emits alert bindings which bias escalation to the top-k stages for that route. 3) Adds a new dashboard focused on cohort drift, stage heatmaps, and per-cohort cost/latency breakdown to help oncall quickly validate root cause hypotheses. 4) Wires the generator into the existing alerting pipeline with a safe canary rollout and automatic quiet-window attenuation to avoid regressing noise. Compatibility and rollout: service defaults to read-only mode until flagged by a feature flag; alert generation starts cross-account in a low-sensitivity mode (only P90/P99) and is then ramped after 72h of monitoring. Testing: unit and integration tests added; ran a 48h synthetic replay against production-like traces (see test run in CI). Checklist: - [x] Unit tests - [x] Integration tests - [x] Dashboard panels - [x] Docs for oncall and runbook - [x] Feature-flagged rollout Plan for operators: deploy to staging -> enable feature flag -> monitor cohort drift and false-positive rate -> bump sensitivity -> full rollout. Summary

This page documents a repeatable, instructor-led bootcamp to train platform operators and engineers to write high-quality runbooks that are telemetry-driven, testable, and maintainable. The curriculum is designed for new operators, service owners, and incident responders who will author or own runbooks for platform services (prefix cache, allocator, tenant-slicing, model-variant router). Audience

- Platform operators and SREs
- Service owners in eng-platform and eng-serving-runtime
- Oncall engineers who respond to latency/cost incidents

Learning objectives (measurable)

The root cause was identified as a known bridging bug in the switch firmware version 1.2.3 [3]. 

Specifically, the "proxy-arp" feature on the edge switch (`edge-sw-7`) was injecting "gratuitous" ARP replies for VPN client IPs into the campus L2 segment, but only when the AP's multicast queue exceeded a 70% threshold [3]. This caused the switch to return ARP responses for the same IP with a different MAC address (matching a spare management interface in rack 7), resulting in the observed duplicate IP warnings and intermittent connectivity blackholes [1, 3].

Summary:
This document describes a recurring class of production incidents we term 'ingress proxy connection entropy' that manifest as intermittent 502/503/504 errors and short spikes of failed model fanout requests. It provides:

- clear symptom definitions and diagnostic queries
- an immediate mitigation runbook for oncall and customer success engineers
- long‑term engineering fixes and rollout guidance
- test and verification checklists for customer-facing cutovers

Scope:
Applies to: Redwood-hosted ingress proxies and customer-managed sidecar proxies that perform request fanout to model serving pools (Hosted, Dedicated, Private).

It provides:

- clear symptom definitions and diagnostic queries
- an immediate mitigation runbook for oncall and customer success engineers
- long‑term engineering fixes and rollout guidance
- test and verification checklists for customer-facing cutovers

Scope:
Applies to: Redwood-hosted ingress proxies and customer-managed sidecar proxies that perform request fanout to model serving pools (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). Not intended for client SDK bugs or pure model runtime failures (see separate model runtime runbooks).

Background and root-cause patterns observed:
We have observed several distinct contributing factors across incidents:

1) Ephemeral port churn + NAT table exhaustion on stateful edge proxies, causing new connections to fail with RST or be reset after TLS handshake.
2) Imbalanced keepalive and health-check interactions where load balancer probes evict live backend sessions during short surges.
3) TLS session cache miss patterns combined with aggressively small client TLS timeouts that increase backend CPU and cause transient overload.
4) Fanout amplification when a single client request fans out to multiple model variants and an upstream slow backend causes head-of-line timeouts.

Symptoms (how customers and SREs will notice this):
- Short, periodic spikes of 502/503/504 errors concentrated to specific ingress proxies (not whole region).
- Error rates correlated to increase in ephemeral port allocation (netstat / ss shows many TIME_WAIT).
- Backend model nodes show normal CPU but elevated accept queue length or connection backlog.
- Trace IDs show upstream TLS handshake succeeded but the first application read returns EOF or ECONNRESET.
- Synthetic journey checks show success for HEAD requests but POST/generation endpoints intermittently fail.

Immediate mitigation runbook (for oncall/customer success):
Priority: restore traffic to customers with minimal impact; preserve telemetry for root-cause analysis.

1) Triage and scope (5–10 minutes)
   - Identify impacted tenants via the error-metrics dashboard (Route: Ingress > proxy-errors by route).
   - Narrow to proxy host(s) using service host labels and trace sampling: search traces for error=502 and group by proxy_hostname.
   - If >50% of requests to a given proxy host are failing, treat as full node degradation.

2) Short-term mitigations (10–30 minutes)
   a) Drain and replace affected proxy instance(s):
      - Mark the proxy node as draining in the autoscaler (CLI):
        kubectl annotate node <proxy-pod> redwood.run/drain=true --overwrite

The recommended two-stage process for rotating signing credentials used by GPU image build and promotion pipelines is as follows:

### **Phase A: Preflight (No live swap)**
The goal of this phase is to test the new credentials without impacting the live environment [1]:
1.  **Provisioning:** Create a new KMS key version and set up an alias (`kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN`) [1].
2.  **Deployment & Testing:** Deploy CI adapters (`sign-image-action`) to use the new key (`key-vN`) in a feature-flagged mode. Perform 100% test-signings that do not alter the promotion ledger, and verify that attestation services accept the new signatures [1].
3.  **Shadow Copying:** Run a shadow cross-account copy using an ephemeral role with the new signing metadata to confirm successful copies across all target regions [1].
4.  **Monitoring:** Monitor for any unexpected pull authentication regressions for 24 hours or three release windows [1].

### **Phase B: Cutover (The swap)**
This phase executes the actual transition [1]:
1.  **Scheduling:** Define a change window with a target "blind window" SLO of less than 30 minutes [1].
2.  **Atomic Swap:** Update the KMS alias (`kms/gpu-image-signer -> key-vN`) [1].
3.  **Revocation:** After a 5-minute grace period, revoke the short-lived CI credentials associated with the previous key version (`key-vN-1`) and rotate ephemeral role sessions [1].
4.  **Canary Verification:** Promote a single canary image signed with the new key (`key-vN`). Monitor canary health across latency and error metrics for 20 minutes [1].
5.  **Full Promotion:** If no triggers are fired during canary verification, proceed to full fleet promotion [1].

### **Rollback Procedures**
**Standard Rollback:**
If issues are detected during the canary phase, revert the alias back to the previous key version (`key-vN-1`) and mark the new key (`key-vN`) as "revocation-pending" for forensic review [1].

**Emergency Rollback (Oncall Steps):**
If a pager fires for mass `pod CrashLoopBackOff` or pull authentication failures, the following immediate actions (within the first 5 minutes) should be taken [1]:
*   **Verify Impact:** Use cross-region registry metrics to determine the percentage of pull auth errors.
*   **Credential Revocation:** If pull auth failures are $\ge$ 3% across $\ge$ 2 regions, run the script: `./scripts/revoke-ci-ephemeral-sessions --role arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/ci-ephemeral-publisher` [1].
*   **Quarantine:** If an image signature mismatch is reported, mark the specific image tag as "blocked" in the promotion ledger [1].

Summary

Purpose
This document defines a safety-first pattern for: (1) rotating CI credentials used by GPU provisioning and image-promotion pipelines, and (2) promoting GPU runtime images (golden bundles) to production pools with provable checks and fast rollback paths. The kit bundles Terraform/IaC patterns, CI job templates, runtime verification checks, SLO-driven gating, and an operator runbook for emergency credential revocation. Why this matters
- Credential rotation without careful orchestration can leave running inference pools unable to pull images, causing degraded capacity and failed deployments. - Image promotion (CI -> staging -> prod) must be atomic and verifiable: a mismatched image in a GPU pool can produce model-regression incidents. - Past incidents show the majority of image-promotion outages occur during key rotation + cross-account image copy windows. This doc reduces blast radius. Scope
Applies to: all CI pipelines that build GPU runtime images, the Terraform modules that provision tenant GPU hosts and warm pools, and the image-signing/attestation services used by Redwood Inference. Owner and contacts
- Owner team: engineering (Infra Reliability)
- Primary oncall for rollout windows: infra-oncall@redwood.com
- Escalation: Diego Ramos (Lead - GPU Infra), Priya Shah (Security), Evan Liu (CI/CD)

Terminology
- Golden image: signed OCI image bundle used for production inference nodes. - Image promoter: CI job that signs, copies, and tags artifacts into the production registry. - Promotion window: the short period where an image transitions from staging to prod and cross-account copies may be in-flight. Safety principles (high level)
1) Always sign images with key versioning (KMS key alias + key-id). Verification must include key version metadata. 2) Use a promotion plan that stages in-region canaries before full fleet promotion. 3) Make credential rotation a two-phase operation: preflight (test) then swap (cutover) with automatic rollback on failure.

answer: The metric name added for counting when the sanitizer finds negative refcounts is **negative-refcount increments** [2].

context_chunks.text: Summary: During a capacity surge on 2025-11-08 we observed a slow but persistent memory growth on several serving nodes which culminated in degraded tail latency and two short-lived OOMs. Investigation showed a new class of 'ghost' entries in the KV prefix cache: entries whose refcount had decayed below zero (underflow) due to an interaction between async compaction, prefetch migration, and a recent refcount optimization. These ghost entries never surfaced as normal cache misses and therefore were not collected by the existing eviction heuristics, leading to gradual slab exhaustion on hot shards. This ticket captures detection heuristics, an emergency snapshot sanitization runbook, a staged rolling-heal design (scheduled drains + isolated snapshot rewrite), telemetry improvements, and a rollout/verification plan. Memory growth first seen 2025-11-06, customer latency degradation at p95/p99 experienced across dedicated and hosted clusters on 2025-11-08. Two nodes hit transient OOMs and auto-recovered (restarts). No persistent data loss; customer requests were served with fallbacks but experienced elevated errors and higher per-token latency. Estimated affected capacity 8% of serving fleet during surge window. Concurrency bug: an optimization in the refcount update path batched decrement operations to reduce atomic ops. Under a race where async compaction rewrites slab bitmaps concurrently with prefetch migrators moving KV records across buckets, the batched decrement could be applied twice for the same logical record. This produced negative refcounts and left entries in an invisible 'ghost' state that bypassed eviction score updates. Compaction also left behind partial tombstone metadata which confused the slab reclaim heuristics. A1: Emergency snapshot sanitization script - implement and run a conservative scanner to detect negative refcounts and mark entries for reclamation. Owner: Marcus Li. Due: 2025-11-18.

Target fleet complete in 72h. Abort conditions: OOMs, persistent error spikes, or eviction backlog growth. Owner: SRE. ## Summary
Runtime 1.22 introduces **KV cache compaction** and **tier-aware KV eviction** to reduce GPU memory fragmentation and mitigate burst-driven tail latency (p95/p99) for sustained decode workloads with mixed sequence lengths. This release adds:
- A **fragmentation-aware allocator health model** (new fragmentation metrics and allocator state tracking). - **Budgeted compaction** (time/bytes) integrated with the scheduler to avoid decode stalls. - A **tier-aware eviction policy** (LRU-by-sequence with safety constraints) to prevent opportunistic/chaotic evictions during bursts. - **Tracing spans and exemplars** to correlate compaction/eviction events with tail latency. - A **kill-switch** and rollout knobs to allow oncall to disable compaction/eviction quickly. Primary expected impact:
- Lower tail latency variance during bursts and churn. - Reduced incidence of “allocator thrash” and fragmentation-driven OOM/forced shedding. - Minimal steady-state throughput impact when budgets are respected. ---

## Who is impacted
**Internal:** Runtime, SRE, Release Engineering, Support, Solutions/CS, Product (Hosted + Dedicated). **External:** Customers on Hosted and Dedicated tiers (and Private if enabled by the account/cluster owner). There are no API surface changes; behavior changes are limited to runtime memory management under load. ---

## What changed (high-level)
### 1) Compaction (new)
The runtime can now **relocate KV pages** to increase contiguity in the KV arena when fragmentation exceeds a trigger threshold. Compaction is incremental and budgeted to limit latency impact. Key properties:
- **Budgeted per scheduler phase** to avoid decode stalls (see “Default settings by tier”). - Uses safe stopping conditions; compaction yields when latency-sensitive work is queued. - Relocation is tracked with counters + traces; correctness is validated under cancellation/churn scenarios.

Scope:
Applies to: Redwood-hosted ingress proxies and customer-managed sidecar proxies that perform request fanout to model serving pools (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). Not intended for client SDK bugs or pure model runtime failures (see separate model runtime runbooks).

Background and root-cause patterns observed:
We have observed several distinct contributing factors across incidents:

1) Ephemeral port churn + NAT table exhaustion on stateful edge proxies, causing new connections to fail with RST or be reset after TLS handshake.
2) Imbalanced keepalive and health-check interactions where load balancer probes evict live backend sessions during short surges.
3) TLS session cache miss patterns combined with aggressively small client TLS timeouts that increase backend CPU and cause transient overload.
4) Fanout amplification when a single client request fans out to multiple model variants and an upstream slow backend causes head-of-line timeouts.

Symptoms (how customers and SREs will notice this):
- Short, periodic spikes of 502/503/504 errors concentrated to specific ingress proxies (not whole region).
- Error rates correlated to increase in ephemeral port allocation (netstat / ss shows many TIME_WAIT).
- Backend model nodes show normal CPU but elevated accept queue length or connection backlog.
- Trace IDs show upstream TLS handshake succeeded but the first application read returns EOF or ECONNRESET.
- Synthetic journey checks show success for HEAD requests but POST/generation endpoints intermittently fail.

Immediate mitigation runbook (for oncall/customer success):
Priority: restore traffic to customers with minimal impact; preserve telemetry for root-cause analysis.

1) Triage and scope (5–10 minutes)
   - Identify impacted tenants via the error-metrics dashboard (Route: Ingress > proxy-errors by route).
   - Narrow to proxy host(s) using service host labels and trace sampling: search traces for error=502 and group by proxy_hostname.
   - If >50% of requests to a given proxy host are failing, treat as full node degradation.

2) Short-term mitigations (10–30 minutes)
   a) Drain and replace affected proxy instance(s):
      - Mark the proxy node as draining in the autoscaler (CLI):
        kubectl annotate node <proxy-pod> redwood.run/drain=true --overwrite
      - Wait for healthy hosts to absorb connections (~30s–2m).
   b) Enable aggressive TCP keepalive tuning for edge proxies (hotfix):
      - For Linux hosts, set: sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1; sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_limit=50; sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=2048
   c) Temporary fanout throttling: switch the fanout policy to sequential or limit to N variants for the affected tenant: update route override in routing-config: 
      - routing-cli set-fanout --route <route> --mode sequential --max-variants 2
   d) If TLS session cache is disabled on the proxy, re-enable with a conservative size (e.g., 10k entries) to reduce handshake load.

3) Customer communication (parallel)
   - Notify affected customers with current scope and ETA: use template 'ingress-interruption-brief' and include mitigations applied and expected next update in 30 minutes.

4) Preserve for RCA (ongoing)
   - Increase trace sampling rate to 25% for the impacted route for the next 2 hours.
   - Capture tcpdump (90s) on affected proxy: sudo tcpdump -w /tmp/proxy-eth0-<ts>.pcap host <client-ip> and upload to incident artifact storage.

Diagnostic steps (deeper root cause analysis):
1) Metrics to query (example PromQL):
   - ingress_proxy_connection_errors_total{code=~"5.."}
   - node_tcp_time_wait_total{instance=~"<host>"}
   - proxy_tls_handshake_duration_seconds_bucket
   - proxy_accept_queue_length{instance=~"<host>"}

2) Log patterns to search (example):
   - "accept: too many open files" in proxy logs
   - "EOF while reading from socket" or "unexpected EOF" in backend service logs
   - Repeated TLS session cache misses (log key: tls_cache_miss=true)

3) Trace analysis approach:
   - Correlate client-side span timestamps to server accept/dispatch spans.

Motivation: users integrating tool/function calling and file uploads via the OpenAI-compatibility endpoints were sending a wide variety of content-types and very large multipart requests which caused inconsistent runtime behavior, high memory pressure, and unexpected acceptance of unsupported payloads. This PR introduces a focused, backwards-compatible implementation for multipart/form-data parsing on the OpenAI-compatibility path, strict Content-Type validation for tool/file inputs, and deterministic payload limits both per-file and per-request. Summary of changes: 1) Add a streaming-safe multipart parser that yields parts rather than buffering entire requests; 2) Validate Content-Type of each part (whitelist: text/*, image/*, application/json, application/octet-stream with explicit size checks); 3) Enforce configurable limits: max_file_size (default 10MiB), max_total_request_size (default 50MiB), max_parts_count (default 20). These defaults are conservative and documented; they can be overridden at tenant or route level via API config. 4) Hook validation into the OpenAI-compat layer so existing client integrations get predictable errors (400/413) with structured error bodies when inputs are rejected. 5) Add detailed unit and integration tests and end-to-end tests for streaming uploads and for the dedicated Dedicated/Private ingress paths. Backwards compatibility notes: this does not change the non-multipart JSON body semantics. Existing users who relied on accepting arbitrary large file uploads should update their tenant config or use Redwood Dedicated with higher quotas. On **2026-01-15**, during a **planned controlled regional failover test** (Hosted API and a limited Dedicated slice) from **us-east** to **eu-west**, we introduced a **customer-visible regression**. A sequence of noisy regional-impairment signals and insufficient rollback/anti-flap guardrails caused repeated routing policy changes (“flip/rollback”) and a transient overload condition in the target region. **Customer impact:**
- **Hosted API:** elevated 5xx/timeouts and tail latency for a subset of routes while traffic re-converged. - **Dedicated:** minimal direct impact due to scoped tenants, but some control-plane operations (drain workflow status) were delayed. - **Streaming:** some clients experienced disconnects on redirect and did not recover cleanly without application-level retries. **Why this postmortem exists:** This was an intentional test. The regression was not catastrophic, but it was **customer-visible** and exposed gaps in our automation safety model. The goal is to make sure controlled testing improves reliability without creating new incidents. ## Severity and scope

The underlying parsing problem was caused by a **leading UTF-8 BOM (0xEF, 0xBB, 0xBF)** being present at the beginning of the "groups" SAML attribute [1]. The server's group-splitting routine used `strings.Split` on the comma and then `TrimSpace`, which successfully removed whitespace but failed to remove the BOM [3]. As a result, the first group name in the list appeared empty or incorrectly formatted to the role-mapper, preventing it from matching the expected admin group (e.g., 'crestline-admins') [1].

The issue was fixed with a server-side patch that runs **`NormalizeUnicode(strip BOM and control chars)`** on the attribute values before the splitting process occurs [3].

Issue summary:
Customer reported that after onboarding to Private VPC (prod-us-east) a subset of their admin users suddenly lost admin privileges and received 403s from the Admin Console APIs. The customers use a SAML IdP (OnPrem SAML 2.0) that sends a 'groups' SAML attribute exported as a single CSV string containing group names. Impact:
- Multiple tenant admins unable to perform admin actions (create API keys, manage billing, role bindings)
- Affects ~6 user accounts in Crestline Analytics (customer-declared admins)
- Production (prod-us-east) only; no impact observed in staging. Environment:
- Redwood Private (customer-managed control plane) deployed in VPC (us-east-1)
- SAML SSO via customer's IdP (SAMLResponse sent to /auth/saml/acs)
- Role mapping configured: first matching group name -> Admin role

Steps to reproduce (as reported):
1) User signs in via SAML SSO. 2) Authn completes and SAMLResponse posted to our ACS. 3) User attempts an admin API call (create api-key). 4) Received 403 Forbidden from Admin API. Observed behavior:
- Successful authentication (session created), but RBAC mapping does not include the expected 'crestline-admins' group for affected users. - Server-side logs show groups attribute present but first group value appears empty when parsed by our role-mapper. Example raw attribute (hex): "EF BB BF 63 72 65 73 74 6C 69 6E 65 2D 61 64 6D 69 6E 73,..." which corresponds to a leading UTF-8 BOM (0xEF,0xBB,0xBF) before 'crestline-admins'. Expected behavior:
- All groups listed in the SAML attribute should be parsed and matched against role mapping rules; admin users should receive the Admin role. Temporary workaround recommended to customer:
- Add a secondary mapping that matches the literal BOM-prefixed group (not ideal). - Alternatively, configure IdP to strip/normalize attribute values prior to assertion export. Notes:
- Customer confirmed IdP was recently upgraded and exported group values using a library that appears to inject a leading BOM on some exports (particularly from their Windows-based AD connector).

Issue summary: Customer reports intermittent 403s for users immediately after the IdP (On-prem SAML IdP) performs a group sync. Impact: Admin and write operations are blocked for some users while they can still view resources. Occurs only in Nimbus Health's private deployment (prod-us-east) and started after their nightly group-sync job. Environment: private deployment (VPC) with SSO proxied through our identity-proxy; session cookies used are SameSite=Lax, cookie named rwd_sess. Customer performed an IdP-side role changeset at 03:40 UTC and ran group sync. Symptoms observed for ~seconds-to-minutes window: some affected users receive 403s for actions requiring newly granted roles while others (or same users after logout/login) succeed. Observed severity: P1 due to business-impacting admin ops during business hours. 1) Customer updates group->role mapping on IdP and triggers IdP group sync. 2) User with existing browser session performs an admin API call (e.g., POST /v1/admin/projects/:id/keys). 3) Server responds 403 with rbac denial. 4) If user logs out and logs back in, call succeeds. Repro rate: intermittent but correlated with IdP sync events. To confirm the disable took effect, check the following:
*   **Config propagation**: Confirm the fleet shows the new effective config [1].
*   **Specific counters/metrics**: Confirm metrics show the expected directional change, specifically **lower compaction time** [1].

## Summary
Runtime 1.22 introduces **KV cache compaction** and **tier-aware KV eviction** to reduce GPU memory fragmentation and mitigate burst-driven tail latency (p95/p99) for sustained decode workloads with mixed sequence lengths. This release adds:
- A **fragmentation-aware allocator health model** (new fragmentation metrics and allocator state tracking). - **Budgeted compaction** (time/bytes) integrated with the scheduler to avoid decode stalls. - A **tier-aware eviction policy** (LRU-by-sequence with safety constraints) to prevent opportunistic/chaotic evictions during bursts. - **Tracing spans and exemplars** to correlate compaction/eviction events with tail latency. - A **kill-switch** and rollout knobs to allow oncall to disable compaction/eviction quickly. Primary expected impact:
- Lower tail latency variance during bursts and churn. - Reduced incidence of “allocator thrash” and fragmentation-driven OOM/forced shedding. - Minimal steady-state throughput impact when budgets are respected. ---

## Who is impacted
**Internal:** Runtime, SRE, Release Engineering, Support, Solutions/CS, Product (Hosted + Dedicated). **External:** Customers on Hosted and Dedicated tiers (and Private if enabled by the account/cluster owner). There are no API surface changes; behavior changes are limited to runtime memory management under load. ---

## What changed (high-level)
### 1) Compaction (new)
The runtime can now **relocate KV pages** to increase contiguity in the KV arena when fragmentation exceeds a trigger threshold. Compaction is incremental and budgeted to limit latency impact. Key properties:
- **Budgeted per scheduler phase** to avoid decode stalls (see “Default settings by tier”). - Uses safe stopping conditions; compaction yields when latency-sensitive work is queued. - Relocation is tracked with counters + traces; correctness is validated under cancellation/churn scenarios.

*   **Metric Label Cardinality Inflation:** The addition of new labels—specifically `kernel_id` and `prompt_bucket`—fragmented the canary's time series into hundreds of unique series [1, 3]. This led to "small-N" slices (low sample counts) that caused the regression evaluator to oscillate between having enough and not enough samples to trigger thresholds [4].
*   **Baseline Drift and Key Mismatch:** There was a mismatch between the canary's emitted metrics and the baseline store's lookup keys [2]. While the baseline store used a key of `model + model_version + sku (+region optional)`, the canary was emitting metrics with extra labels; because the lookup did not strip these extra labels, the system frequently failed to find the correct baseline ("baseline not found"), causing the evaluator to fall back to default or zero values [2, 3, 4].
*   **Deduplication Failure:** The `incident-bot` dedupe keys lacked stable identifiers (specifically for `model, version, region, sku, runtime_build`), which caused the same underlying symptom to create repeated parallel threads and pages [4].

### **Immediate Mitigations and Config Changes**
To stop the repeated pages and stabilize the signal, the following actions were taken:
*   **Silencing Alerts:** Rafael Mendes applied a silence in Alertmanager for `perf-canary-*page*` rules for a duration of one hour [3].
*   **Disabling Paging Rules:** SREs disabled the paging rules in `observability-pack` while keeping warnings active [4].
*   **Increasing Dampening:** The dampening window was increased to mitigate noise [4].
*   **Canary Rollback:** The canary configuration was rolled back to the previous 3-model set, which successfully dropped the alert volume [4].

answer:
The intermittent 403 RBAC denials in the private VPC deployment were caused by the **identity-proxy caching role assertions** keyed by the SAML `session_index` for performance [1]. Because the `session_index` remains stable across IdP group syncs, the cache was not invalidated when groups were updated, causing existing sessions to return a **stale cached role set** (e.g., `team:viewer`) instead of the newly granted roles (e.g., `team:admin`) until the cache expired [1, 2].

The following solutions were applied:
*   **Mitigation:** An immediate **cache eviction** was implemented upon receiving IdP `user-change` webhooks for the affected user or `session_index` [2].
*   **Long-term server-side fix:** The fix involved adding an **immediate cache eviction** on receiving IdP user-change webhooks for the affected user/session_index [2].

answer:
The root cause of the March 2026 incident was a **race condition in the `sse-gateway`** [2]. Specifically, when an upstream TCP RST (caused by an edge-proxy idle probe) occurred mid-flight, an in-flight terminal chunk flush and a scheduled keepalive/heartbeat could be interleaved [2]. This led to the terminal 'end' event being dropped and the gateway retransmitting heartbeat frames that were then interleaved with the resumed payload during a client's immediate retry/resume attempt [1, 2].

The server-side fix involved rolling out **PR 2147**, which included the following resolutions:
*   **Atomic Emission:** Forced the atomic emission of the terminal 'end' event [1, 2].
*   **Frame Ordering:** Ensured stronger ordering of frames by placing heartbeat frames behind the terminal flush [1, 2].
*   **Backoff Implementation:** Applied a short backoff on client resume acceptance to better tolerate in-flight socket tear-downs [2].

Context: production customers observed cases where long lived streaming sessions (tool calls + structured output) were left in indeterminate states after a client network disconnect or a client-initiated Cancel. Motivation: we need a predictable server-side safety net that bounds resource residency time, ensures tool-call idempotency when retries/resume occur, and provides a clear fallback path (trimmed response + final event) that OpenAI-compatible clients can rely on. This PR implements a server-side streaming timebox (configurable per-route) that gracefully converts oversized/inflight streams into a final 'timeboxed' terminal event, augments client-cancel handling to be idempotent across reconnect/resume windows, and plumbs a compact resume token that includes tool-call idempotency metadata. Summary of changes: 1) stream manager: add configurable timebox_ms and a deterministic finalization path that emits a structured terminal event ("__redwood_timeboxed__") with a compact summary; 2) openai adapter: interpret Cancel events as idempotent markers tied to resume tokens; retries within the resume window will deduplicate tool calls using a request-level id; 3) tooling: map function-call invocations to idempotency keys and persist minimal call metadata to the stream checkpoint to support safe resume; 4) API: extend the OpenAI-compat streaming spec with two optional fields in the final event (timeboxed=true, resume_hint) without breaking existing clients; 5) tests & docs: integration tests for flaky network simulated disconnects and release notes for the behavior and recommended operational knobs. Rollout plan: feature guarded behind a runtime flag and route-level config. Backwards compatibility: default behavior is unchanged unless a route opts-in. After the Console v4.3.2 rollout, the reversion of saved dashboard filter presets to the default was caused by the frontend emitting a `presets:clear` event when a sub-report save returned a 200 status [1, 2]. Provide a secure, role-aware bulk dump capability for audit logs from the Console that supports CSV, JSON, and NDJSON outputs while respecting RBAC v2 filters, retention policies, and SSO-backed admin permissions. The goal is to let enterprise admins and compliance teams extract query-scoped audit slices (time-window, actor, resource, action, outcome) for offline analysis and e-discovery without exposing redacted fields to users who lack privileges. Must handle multi-GB exports via cursored incremental downloads, enforce rate and size limits, and produce manifest metadata (query, applied filters, snapshot_time, schema_version).

- Deterministic intent: include all inputs that can affect output (tokenizer, seed, model artifact id, runtime config, injected policies). - Portable: JSON-compatible, human-readable, and easy to attach to support tickets or GitHub issues. - Privacy-aware: fields that may contain PII must be flagged and optionally replaced with redaction pointers. Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

Environment (examples):
- host_os: ubuntu-22.04
- runtime_image: redwood/runtime-infer:2025-10-21
- gpu: a100-80gb (or cpu)
- region: us-west-2
- concurrency_profile: \"single-req\" | \"batched\"

Telemetry references:
These are URIs (or internal artifact ids) pointing to:
- structured trace (jaeger/span id)
- token-level metrics (latency per token)
- server logs (filtered range)
- resource utilization snapshot (GPU memory thread dump)

Privacy notes:
- raw_payload_ref should be used in combination with privacy_policy.

*   **Metrics window:** A window covering 30 minutes before the incident, the duration of the incident, and 2 hours after the incident.

- clear symptom definitions and diagnostic queries

Scope:
Applies to: Redwood-hosted ingress proxies and customer-managed sidecar proxies that perform request fanout to model serving pools (Hosted, Dedicated, Private).

Scope:
Applies to: Redwood-hosted ingress proxies and customer-managed sidecar proxies that perform request fanout to model serving pools (Hosted, Dedicated, Private). Not intended for client SDK bugs or pure model runtime failures (see separate model runtime runbooks).

Background and root-cause patterns observed:
We have observed several distinct contributing factors across incidents:

1) Ephemeral port churn + NAT table exhaustion on stateful edge proxies, causing new connections to fail with RST or be reset after TLS handshake.
2) Imbalanced keepalive and health-check interactions where load balancer probes evict live backend sessions during short surges.
3) TLS session cache miss patterns combined with aggressively small client TLS timeouts that increase backend CPU and cause transient overload.
4) Fanout amplification when a single client request fans out to multiple model variants and an upstream slow backend causes head-of-line timeouts.

Symptoms (how customers and SREs will notice this):
- Short, periodic spikes of 502/503/504 errors concentrated to specific ingress proxies (not whole region).
- Error rates correlated to increase in ephemeral port allocation (netstat / ss shows many TIME_WAIT).
- Backend model nodes show normal CPU but elevated accept queue length or connection backlog.
- Trace IDs show upstream TLS handshake succeeded but the first application read returns EOF or ECONNRESET.
- Synthetic journey checks show success for HEAD requests but POST/generation endpoints intermittently fail.

Immediate mitigation runbook (for oncall/customer success):
Priority: restore traffic to customers with minimal impact; preserve telemetry for root-cause analysis.

1) Triage and scope (5–10 minutes)
   - Identify impacted tenants via the error-metrics dashboard (Route: Ingress > proxy-errors by route).
   - Narrow to proxy host(s) using service host labels and trace sampling: search traces for error=502 and group by proxy_hostname.
   - If >50% of requests to a given proxy host are failing, treat as full node degradation.

2) Short-term mitigations (10–30 minutes)
   a) Drain and replace affected proxy instance(s):
      - Mark the proxy node as draining in the autoscaler (CLI):
        kubectl annotate node <proxy-pod> redwood.run/drain=true --overwrite
      - Wait for healthy hosts to absorb connections (~30s–2m).
   b) Enable aggressive TCP keepalive tuning for edge proxies (hotfix):
      - For Linux hosts, set: sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse=1; sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_tw_limit=50; sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog=2048

## Summary
On **2026-01-15**, during a **planned controlled regional failover test** (Hosted API and a limited Dedicated slice) from **us-east** to **eu-west**, we introduced a **customer-visible regression**. A sequence of noisy regional-impairment signals and insufficient rollback/anti-flap guardrails caused repeated routing policy changes (“flip/rollback”) and a transient overload condition in the target region. **Customer impact:**
- **Hosted API:** elevated 5xx/timeouts and tail latency for a subset of routes while traffic re-converged. - **Dedicated:** minimal direct impact due to scoped tenants, but some control-plane operations (drain workflow status) were delayed. - **Streaming:** some clients experienced disconnects on redirect and did not recover cleanly without application-level retries. **Why this postmortem exists:** This was an intentional test. The regression was not catastrophic, but it was **customer-visible** and exposed gaps in our automation safety model. The goal is to make sure controlled testing improves reliability without creating new incidents. ## Severity and scope
- **Incident type:** Planned test causing unplanned customer-visible regression
- **Severity:** SEV-2 (customer-visible errors for a limited subset; short duration; mitigated quickly)
- **Services impacted:** Hosted API (gateway + smart routing), failover automation controller, region health evaluation pipeline
- **Regions:** us-east (source), eu-west (target)

## Customer impact (what users experienced)
- Transient **HTTP 5xx** and **gateway timeouts** during the flip/rollback window. - Elevated **p95/p99 latency** for successful requests during the same interval. - Some **streaming sessions** dropped when redirected cross-region; a subset of clients did not resume streaming until they retried from the application. Notes:
- We did not publish an external status page incident because this was a planned test with limited blast radius; however, **Support received inbound tickets** from customers who noticed errors during the window.

The root cause and the immediate mitigations for the us-east canary incident are as follows:

**Root Cause**
The issue was caused by a cookie domain normalization (rewrite) during the canary rollout, which changed the cookie scope (from host-scoped to `Domain=.redwood.ai`) [1]. This caused the **session-manager** to treat existing sessions as "orphaned," leading to a **COOKIE_DOMAIN_MISMATCH** that evicted the pinned model version and forced the router to use a fallback model [1]. The problem specifically affected long-poll streaming clients that reused old host-scoped cookies without immediately refreshing their session metadata [1].

**Immediate Mitigations**
*   **Platform-side:** Engineers rolled back the cookie-domain rewrite for the canary cohort [2]. Additionally, a defensive guard was added to the session-manager to allow it to accept equivalent cookie scopes for pinned sessions when domain normalization occurs [2].
*   **Customer-side:** The customer (BrightChat) was instructed to force a session refresh (using `POST /v1/sessions/refresh`) [1, 2]. This allowed pinned routing to be restored within approximately two minutes for the refreshed sessions [1, 2].

- Deterministic intent: include all inputs that can affect output (tokenizer, seed, model artifact id, runtime config, injected policies). - Portable: JSON-compatible, human-readable, and easy to attach to support tickets or GitHub issues. - Privacy-aware: fields that may contain PII must be flagged and optionally replaced with redaction pointers. Top-level fields (v1):
- manifest_id: short id (UUID recommended)
- created_by: name/email of the authoring agent (person, system)
- created_at: ISO date
- source_context: freeform string describing the scenario (UI flow, API route)
- requests: ordered list of request descriptors (see below)
- environment: runtime/environment snapshot (hardware/host tags, region, container image)
- model_artifact: model id + exact artifact checksum (sha256) + quantization profile id
- tokenizer: tokenizer version id + checksum + tokenizer config (if nonstandard)
- runtime_flags: map-like list of runtime knobs that influence execution (e.g., use_kv_cache=false)
- deterministic_seeds: list of PRNG seeds used for sampling or other non-deterministic logic
- telemetry_refs: pointers to associated logs, traces, and metric snapshots
- privacy_policy: small token describing redaction level (none, partial, strict)
- signature: optional signed blob for integrity verification (OIDC/JWKS compatible)

Request descriptor (ordered list element):
- request_id: short id (monotonic in manifest)
- timestamp: ISO timestamp of original request
- api_route: e.g., \"/v1/generate\" or \"/v1/chat/completions\"
- client_sdk: client library and version (if applicable)
- raw_payload_ref: pointer to stored payload (S3/GCS/secure-store) OR inline (redacted) string
- input_checksums: list of checksum objects (tokenization checksum, raw text checksum)
- sampling_config: temperature/top_k/top_p/typical_p/seed (if used)
- pre_hooks: list of transformations (name@version + diff/checksum) applied by client or proxy
- post_hooks: list of response transformations (e.g., de-identification, markup)
- expected_response_signature: optional small fingerprint of the original response to enable quick divergence checks
- fallback_policy_trace: if fallback occurred during original call (e.g., switched to smaller model), record decisions and timestamps

Environment (examples):
- host_os: ubuntu-22.04
- runtime_image: redwood/runtime-infer:2025-10-21
- gpu: a100-80gb (or cpu)

- concurrency_profile: \"single-req\" | \"batched\"

The confirmed root cause was a **catalog alias persistence bug** during a migration/promotion flow [3]. Specifically, the migration script (PR #2731) failed to write tenant-specific alias overrides for a subset of tenants due to a **race condition**, causing the `open-embed-default` alias to unexpectedly resolve to the new 1024-d model (`open-embed-1024-v2`) instead of the expected legacy 512-d model (`open-embed-512-v1`) [2, 3].

The deployment of fixes and mitigations included:
